A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OptiBench benchmark, ReSocratic synthesis method, and ReSocratic-29K dataset. Their complete main texts, appendices, tables, figures, and mathematical content support comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v2 reports original model evaluations, supervised fine-tuning results, synthesis ablations, and forward-versus-reverse synthesis comparisons in Tables 2-4, plus NL4OPT-E evaluations in Appendix A.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds model evaluations, error analysis, prompting experiments, Pass@k results, runtime comparisons, and human assessments in Appendices B and C.

M1.justification: The proposed three-stage ReSocratic pipeline, rule and similarity filters, question/code translation, and supervised fine-tuning procedure remain unchanged. The original synthesis and evaluation prompts are retained. Additional reasoning-first and problem-expansion experiments are presented as supplementary studies rather than revisions to the synthesis pipeline.

E1.justification: OptiBench, NL4OPT-E, and ReSocratic-29K retain their existing coverage. v4 Appendix B.5 adds a limited problem-expansion scenario: DeepSeek-V2.5 must enlarge an existing optimization problem's variables and constraints, with ten expanded samples evaluated by humans. No additional benchmark or application domain is evaluated.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds evaluated comparisons with Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, Qwen2-7B-Instruct, DeepSeek-V2.5, GPT-4o-mini, and GPT-4o. Its few-shot block drops Llama-3-70B, DeepSeek-V2, GPT-3.5-Turbo, and GPT-4; the latter two retain aggregate results in Table 9. v4 also introduces reasoning-first prompting comparisons and human-written code as a runtime comparator. The Self-Instruct and Evol-Instruct synthesis comparisons remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The original answer-accuracy evaluation and fine-tuning settings remain stable. New protocols include DeepSeek-V2.5 judging mathematical formulations, a separate formulation-to-code accuracy measure, reasoning-first prompting, Pass@5 through Pass@30 at temperature 0.7, and runtime comparisons restricted to correctly solved instances. Separate human assessments validate judge agreement, expanded problems, and back-translations.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained filter and step-question ablations, v4 adds substantial diagnostic evidence: formulation-versus-coding error analysis and two coding-error cases, prompting sensitivity, multiple-attempt performance, generated-code efficiency, and problem-expansion feasibility in Appendix B. Appendix C.3 separately checks back-translation fidelity. These investigate failure sources and component reliability absent from v2.

E5.justification: Neither version reports random seeds, uncertainty across replicated experiments, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v4's Pass@k results vary the candidate-generation budget rather than estimate run-to-run uncertainty. Its human assessments report raw agreement or correctness counts, retaining the point-estimate reporting practice already used for synthetic-data accuracy in v2.

E6.justification: v4 adds numerous results, including GPT-4o accuracy of 66.1% zero-shot and 69.4% few-shot in Table 2, making it the strongest reported overall comparator. New findings include lower accuracy with reasoning-first prompting, increasing Pass@k, 19/20 human-judge agreement, 9/10 valid problem expansions, and 20/20 correct back-translations. Shared SFT results remain 30.6% and 51.1%, and Tables 3-5 retain their numerical results.

T1.justification: The formal evaluation construction and existing mathematical formulations are retained. Neither version develops a theoretical analysis with theorems or proofs. The additional optimization formulations in v4 serve as empirical examples and prompt demonstrations rather than new theoretical results.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same central claims: a 605-question benchmark covering linear, nonlinear, and tabular optimization; reverse Socratic data synthesis; and improved open-model performance through ReSocratic-29K fine-tuning. The additional evidence does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v4 substantially expands interpretation beyond v2's difficulty-by-data-type discussion. Appendix B attributes failures to mathematical reasoning and solver-specific coding limitations, and interprets runtime comparisons as locating the main bottleneck in correctness rather than execution efficiency. It also presents problem expansion as a possible basis for future self-improvement. Appendix C.3 explains back-translation as largely extracting the demonstration's natural-language content.

D1.justification: v4 newly specifies annotator qualifications, a six-person team, four independent annotations per question, and adjudication procedures in Appendix D.1. It supplies exact reasoning-first and LLM-judge prompts in Appendix E. Existing training hardware, hyperparameters, data formats, and synthesis prompts are retained or relocated. Conversely, v2's project code/data link and contest access links are removed; this does not establish that the resources themselves became unavailable.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds Chen and Lampouras (2023) and Xie et al. (2023), distinguishing ReSocratic's stepwise reverse construction from back-translation-based augmentation. References also add Gose, Scholle, Mistral, and Qwen2 sources. These are focused additions; the broader positioning against existing optimization benchmarks and forward synthesis remains stable.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose and the principal section order remain unchanged. v4 shortens the main annotation description, moves the training-message format to Appendix C.4, and reorganizes the appendices around a new experimental section. It also makes limited wording edits and updates affiliations, conference headers, and acknowledgments.

P2.justification: Table 2 is expanded and its comparator rows reorganized. Six new tables, Tables 6-11, present error decomposition, prompting comparisons, Pass@k, and runtime results, substantially extending the displayed evidence. Figures 1-8 are retained, with several figures and tables relocated or resized within the revised layout.

improvement.justification: v4 makes benchmark performance more interpretable through formulation-versus-coding diagnostics, broader baseline comparisons, and targeted human checks that were absent from v2. These benefits are limited by small audit samples and incomplete integration: Section 5.3 still calls GPT-4 strongest despite Table 2 favoring GPT-4o. Removing the code/data access link also weakens reproducibility guidance. The added evidence supports a net improvement, while the central synthesis and fine-tuning evidence remains unchanged.
